title: Structural Evolution of Au-Ag Core-Shell Nanoparticles Under Electron Beam Exposure: Insights into Atomic Migration and Alloy Formation
content: Bimetallic nanoparticles have garnered significant interest in recent years due to their versatile applications across diverse fields, including medicine, biology, pharmaceuticals, cell signaling, catalysis, and more [1]. These nanoparticles possess unique physicochemical properties that arise from the combination of two different metallic elements, enabling them to outperform their monometallic counterparts in many applications. Among the various configurations of bimetallic nanoparticles, two of the most extensively studied are the core-shell type and the nanoalloy type, both of which have been widely explored for their enhanced functionality in the aforementioned areas [2]. The structural arrangement of atoms within nanoparticles plays a crucial role in determining their properties, such as optical behavior, catalytic activity, magnetic response, and thermal stability. This structural organization directly influences their potential for practical applications, making it a subject of intense research interest [3]. For instance, in Au-Ag core-shell nanoparticles, the distinct separation of the core and shell materials often leads to a combination of properties that can be tailored for specific uses. Gaining insights into these transitions could provide valuable information for the development of novel synthesis techniques. One promising approach involves the use of electron microscopy to closely monitor and manipulate the growth and transformation of nanoparticles at the atomic level. In this study, gold-silver (Au-Ag) core-shell nanoparticles were synthesized using the chemical reduction method [4]. The synthesis process began with the preparation of the gold (Au) core. A 0.1 mM solution of chloroauric acid was stirred at room temperature using a magnetic stirrer to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, 2 mL of a 5 mM sodium borohydride solution was added as a reducing agent to facilitate the formation of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs). The resulting dispersion of AuNPs served as the core for the subsequent shell formation. To synthesize the silver (Ag) shell, a 1 mM silver nitrate solution (5 µL) and a 10 mM sodium borohydride solution (20 µL) were sequentially added to the Au nanoparticle dispersion under continuous stirring. This process led to the formation of Au-Ag core-shell nanoparticles. The synthesized nanoparticles were characterized using a JEOL JEM-2100 transmission electron microscope (TEM), operated at a constant accelerating voltage of 200 kV. TEM analysis was conducted to investigate the structural and morphological properties of the nanoparticles. Additionally, the Au nanoparticles were subjected to electron beam exposure at varying time intervals (from 0 to 120 s) to evaluate the behavior of atoms within the nanoparticles.
